newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Canny Dutch take Fiat baby to their hearts.
newsitem.headline: Canny Dutch take Fiat baby to their hearts.

text.p: Parked end-on to the pavement, as they often are in Amsterdam, a tiny Fiat Cinquecento takes up less than half the kerbspace of the average family car.
That's why canny Amsterdammers are finding their way to Henk ten Cate's Fiat 500 business which imports, sells and services the classic Italian cars launched by Fiat in the 1950s.

As parking restrictions in Dutch cities bite harder and harder and frustrated drivers spend ever longer cruising around looking for parking spaces, the Cinquecento has become prized for its ability to squeeze into the tightest spot.

"I never have to leave my Cinquecento more than 40 metres (yards) away from the place I want to go to," said Ten Cate. "That makes a big difference, especially when you see people riding round in circles looking for somewhere to park."

Amsterdam's merciless parking authorities, who can clamp an illegally parked car in the time it takes to nip into a shop and buy a newspaper, often turn a blind eye to cheekily parked Cinquecentos, says Ten Cate.
"I've left my car in all sorts of places, as long as you buy a parking ticket and don't leave it where it could be dangerous the authorities don't pay much attention," he said.

At just 1.3 metres (four feet) wide and three metres (yards) long the egg-shaped auto is even small enough to squeeze between the "Amsterdammertje" bollards which line the canals to keep cars off the pavements.
"I don't think the council took the Cinquecento into account when it set the distance between Amsterdammertjes," he said, "It's got to be the narrowest car on the roads here."
Ten Cate says he has no problem fitting his 1.96-metre (six foot) frame into the 1.3 metre (four feet) high Fiat but says he wouldn't advise trying to squeeze four adults into the car.
Ten Cate, 44, who trained as a doctor but never practised, fell in love with the Fiat baby on visits to Italy as a student, and decided to try and sell them in his native Holland.
"I realised that I didn't have the patience to listen to the patients -- I like having my own business, I love Italy and I love these cars so it seemed logical," he said.
DUTCH BABY FIATS A HEALTHY IMPORT BUSINESS
Amsterdammers were so entranced by the first Cinquecento he brought to the Dutch capital about 12 years ago that he sold his first one to a man who flagged him down on the street.

He estimates he has sold about 400 Cinquecentos since then, and has built up his business to the point that he now sells around 40 of the nippy roadsters a year -- visiting Italy six times a year to pick up fresh stock.
The Dutch Fiat 500 club, set up in 1980, boasts around 3,000 members throughout the Netherlands, although Ten Cate reckons about 4,000 of the cars currently ply Dutch roads.
Importing the cars is probably less lucrative than servicing and maintaining them, as people from miles around flock to him with their problems, Ten Cate says.

Although Fiat ended production of the cars in the mid-1970s Ten Cate says he has no problem picking out dozens of Cinquecentos in Italy. Fiat still makes engines for the cars in Poland and other parts are available in Italy.
While the bicycle gives the ultimate freedom of movement in the Dutch capital, some people can't or won't give up their cars and for them the Cinquecento is ideal.

"A lot of people in business who have lots of appointments in different parts of the city find the Cinquecento attractive," said Ten Cate, adding that estate agents often used them to ferry clients to and from properties.
CHEEKY CHARM OF CINQUECENTO WINS CUSTOMERS
The impish charm of the Fiat baby, the descendent of the "Topolino" or Mickey Mouse car created by Fiat designer Dante Giacosa and introduced in the 1930s, is not lost on the Dutch.
Ten Cate says most of his customers are drawn by the jaunty little car's style and simplicity. "People just like the shape. It's not like modern cars which all look the same," he said.
Dutch Cinquecento owners are also intensely loyal, with some of Ten Cate's customers on their fifth or sixth little Fiat, although many have a bigger more modern car for long journeys.
"If someone came to me and said they needed a car to travel to The Hague (50 km or 30 miles from Amsterdam) I wouldn't recommend a 500, they're just not that comfortable for long trips," he said.

And the famously economical Dutch are equally gratified that they can pick up a Cinquecento for as little as 1,000 guilders ($560) although a fully refurbished, resprayed Cinquecento with a brand new engine will set them back 12,000 guilders.

For that sort of money Ten Cate will spray it any colour you like, ranging from an eye-aching yellow to a sombre blue. He has even arranged for one to be turned into a moving Picasso and can, at the flick of an acetylene torch, fix you a cabriolet.
"A lot of people actually don't want to attract attention because sun roofs make these cars easy too break into."
But a simple break-in pales in comparison to the creeping horror which haunts Cinquecento owners in Amsterdam.
"Every now and then you hear about a bunch of lads getting drunk, picking up a Cinquecento and dropping it in a canal. It has been known to happen," he said. ($1=1.779 Guilder)
